title: Anointing and viaticum
hookLine: the last communion is food for the journey
tomorrow: what makes a death "happy"? Abuela's answer has three names.

cards: Some families treat the hospital chaplain like bad news: call the priest, and Grandma will think it's the end. Others call the day a diagnosis lands. Who's right?
Inside the Church, both instincts have a case, because there are really two gifts here: an anointing, and a last meal for the road.

teach.h: LET HIM BRING IN THE PRIESTS.

teach.b: The letter of James says, in the Douay-Rheims Bible: "Is any man sick among you? Let him bring in the priests of the church, and let them pray over him, anointing him with oil in the name of the Lord."
For a long time it was saved for the very end and called extreme unction, the last anointing.

teach.h: CALL EARLY: NOT ONLY AT THE END.
teach.b: The call-early side points to the Second Vatican Council, which said this sacrament isn't only for those at the point of death, and named it the anointing of the sick.
Call when serious illness begins; it can be given again.
Wait for the last hour, and the person may no longer be awake to receive it. The wait side has its own case, and it's about the second gift.
Viaticum is the Church's word for the last communion given to someone who is dying. It belongs to the end, and families who wait are guarding something real: hope, and a sick person's peace.

teach.h: ARISE, EAT: A GREAT WAY TO GO.
teach.b: Here's one to tell a friend: the old picture for viaticum is Elijah, worn out in the desert, woken by an angel: "Arise, eat: for thou hast yet a great way to go." Both sides agree on that bread.
The anointing can come early; the food for the way comes at the end.

how: A priest anoints a seriously ill person's forehead and hands with blessed oil, often at home or in the hospital, and the sacrament can be repeated; near death, a priest or extraordinary minister brings viaticum, the last communion.

practice: Find the phone number of the nearest Catholic parish or hospital chaplain, and save it under a name you'd recognize in a hurry. Then let the sit be quiet. If you pray, hold in mind someone who may need that number before you do.

wordCard.voice: Viaticum. The last communion, given to someone who is dying: food for the way.

orig.note: Latin: provisions for a journey. the Church's word for the last communion.

carryVoice: Here's the line: food for the way, like the bread an angel set beside Elijah. Until tomorrow.
